title: Emerson's limits
hookLine: critics say his optimism skips over evil and suffering

cards: Read enough Emerson in one sitting and a question starts to press. The stars are a revelation. Every act rewards or punishes itself.
Trust thyself and the universe will meet you. Nothing can bring you peace but yourself. It's bracing.

It's lovely. Then you put the book down and turn on the news, or sit in a hospital waiting room, or remember what was happening in his own country while he wrote. Where, in all that light, is the dark?
Readers have asked that about Emerson for a long time. Today, the case against him, told fairly, and what's still standing after it.

teach.h: THE CHARGE: IT SKIPS OVER EVIL.
BRIGHT PAGES IN A DARK TIME.
teach.b: Some critics, in his time and since, say Emerson's optimism skips over evil. His essay Compensation says every act comes back to its doer, but innocent people suffer for things they never did.

The Over-Soul holds every life in something larger, but that can sound distant to someone in pain. And a philosophy built on self-trust has little to say to someone whose self has been broken by illness or cruelty.
Second, his own country. Emerson wrote his brightest pages while slavery was the law in much of it, and, as this path saw a few days ago, he was slow to speak.
Critics ask whether a sunny view of the soul made it easier to look away. Third, the defense, and it's real.

Emerson knew grief. He lost his young wife, brothers he loved, and his little son, after whose death he wrote that grief could teach him nothing. That's not the sentence of a man who never looked into the dark.
Later essays face limits head on, the things a person cannot will away. His hope wasn't naive so much as stubborn. Fourth, the useful middle.
Both can be true. His hope is a real gift, and it has edges where it stops working.

teach.h: A GOOD MAP WITHOUT EVERY CLIFF.
teach.b: Carry it the way a hiker carries a good map that doesn't show every cliff: use it, love it, know where it ends.
Hope with limits isn't weaker hope. It's hope that has been honest about the waiting room.

how: Readers and teachers of Emerson often pair his hopeful essays with the criticism that they pass too lightly over evil and suffering, and with his own writing on grief and limits.

practice: In one open hand, picture an Emerson line from these weeks: trust thyself, under the stars, another circle. In the other, picture something his line can't reach: a loss, an injustice, someone whose suffering no essay touches.
Let neither hand close and neither cancel the other; just sit with both open, side by side.

wordCard.voice: Emerson's limits. The critics' charge that his optimism skips over evil and suffering, and the honest answer that his hope is real and also has edges. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: hope with limits. A good map still has edges. Rest well.
